content: Decisions made by the Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS) are explained in the appraisal. The chemical composition and properties of the technical-grade active ingredient are typically assessed using data from five-batch analyses, which include information on purity, impurities, the minimum active ingredient content (with tolerances for technical concentrates), maximum levels of relevant impurities, and the identities and limits of stabilizers or essential additives. Physical properties such as melting point, boiling point, and decomposition temperature are also evaluated. If these data influence JMPS decisions, the rationale is included in the appraisal. Toxicological and ecotoxicological background information is summarized based on evaluations conducted by other organizations. This information is not typically re-evaluated unless it directly impacts JMPS decisions. The manufacturer’s statement on toxicological data is included, along with a summary of the main formulation types available and the countries where these formulations are registered and sold. Methods used to analyze and test physicochemical properties are briefly summarized. These include techniques for determining the identity of the active ingredient (using at least two independent methods), its content, relevant impurities, and physical test methods. The validation status of these methods is stated, and any incomplete validations are identified in the appraisal. Special requirements for containers and packaging are briefly noted but not evaluated. A hazard summary provided by the proposer includes information on acute, sub-acute, and chronic toxicity (including carcinogenicity and teratogenicity), genotoxicity, and ecotoxicology derived from the technical-grade active ingredient. If data on the toxicity of relevant impurities are available, they are included. Evaluations conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO) or institutions nominated by WHO are summarized in the appraisal if they assist in determining equivalence; otherwise, this information is not evaluated or summarized. References to published and unpublished documents containing data or information presented in the report are included. Unpublished documents are referenced by study number, authors, year, and title, along with a document number allocated by the sponsor. Emails are referenced by author, date, sender’s organization, and FAO/WHO recipient. To protect authors and laboratories, identifying details may be omitted. The JMPS assesses impurity, toxicological, and ecotoxicological profiles to determine which impurities are relevant and must be specified. FAO/WHO agrees on the text of the evaluation and specification, and the proposer verifies its factual accuracy. FAO/WHO then publishes the evaluation and specification, including the names of the proposers of the specifications for technical-grade active ingredients or formulations recommended for adoption. Data requirements and procedures are outlined for cases where insufficient data are provided, the quality of the material is unacceptable, or changes to the specification are needed. Actions range from rejecting the submission to revising the specification in collaboration with the proposer. FAO and WHO prioritize their three-year program for developing and reviewing specifications based on criteria such as health or environmental hazards, re-evaluation by regulatory authorities, or changes in manufacturing processes. Specifications aim to describe quantifiable parameters with defined limits, avoiding subjective judgment by the buyer. Technical-grade active ingredients should be as pure as economically feasible to minimize formulation and toxicity issues. The JMPS considers technical challenges in raising quality standards but often prioritizes long-term benefits of improved quality. Formulation specifications consider properties relevant to efficacy, operator safety, and environmental impact. Standard tests may not exist for all parameters, necessitating the development of new methods or improvement of existing ones. Specifications for formulations typically refer to a single active ingredient. For co-formulated products, specifications must address the purity and impurity content of each active ingredient. Analytical methods must be validated, and the specification will not be published until validation is complete. Tolerances for active ingredient content are based on manufacturing, sampling, and analytical variations. Positive deviations from upper limits may be allowed if justified by the need to compensate for storage degradation. For solid formulations, expanded tolerances account for the challenges of achieving homogeneity compared to liquid mixtures.
